## Reading the ES line properly, and what the full readings moved

*2026-09-15 18:40:28 · record*

Six papers now, read end to end rather than by abstract. Four things the
readings changed that the earlier passes had wrong, missing, or filed on
trust.

**The scale evidence was understated and the independence was overstated —
in the same paper.** `LIT-234` runs evolution strategies at 14B and 32B
against OatZero and SimpleRL-Zoo, which is four times the ceiling `SOTA-154`'s
conditions section claimed. It is also Cognizant AI Lab with Qiu among the
authors, running `LIT-211`'s own method — the case that practice's promotion
condition explicitly excluded. **Both facts are load-bearing and they point
opposite ways**, and the temptation on finding either is to let it settle the
question alone. The practice now carries the 32B number *and* the sentence
"the independent evidence stops at 8B", because a reader needs both to know
what they are looking at.

That is the same error as the last pass in a new costume. Then it was refusing
evidence for a category the condition never named; here it would have been
accepting evidence the condition named and excluded, because the number was
impressive. **A condition is only worth writing if it binds in the direction
you did not want.**

**The dissent and the characterization are arguing about one measurement.**
`LIT-231` proves that random perturbations concentrate near orthogonality
to a useful direction, and that the leftover components accumulate as a random
walk — so ES cannot work at LLM scale. `LIT-230`, four months later,
measures that exact drift, agrees it is 40× GRPO's, and finds it harmless:
the gains survive zeroing every update below a single-step magnitude
threshold, so they live in a sparse coordinate subset — and in a *specific*
one, LayerNorm weights and attention projections, where GRPO's largest updates
land in token embeddings and the language-model head instead.

The gap between them is a line and a subspace. Lemma 1 bounds the angle
between a random vector and a single direction; if the useful set is a
`k`-dimensional subspace, the projection behaves differently and the argument
weakens by an amount nobody has computed. That is written into both readings
as an open question. **It is not written in as a refutation, because working
out which of two papers is right from a third document is how a record starts
believing its own summaries.**

There is a second, sharper tension neither paper notices: Hyper-ES's lemmas
are dimension-asymptotic, so read naively they predict ES gets *worse* with
scale, while every empirical paper in the line reports the opposite and
`THEORY-006` says why it should. Something in that argument does not
track the observation. Saying so is the useful contribution here; saying which
is not available yet.

**A prediction was confirmed and the promotion condition still was not met.**
`THEORY-006` asked for the density measurement repeated by an unconnected
group on a family other than Qwen2.5, or a mechanism predicting where the
transition sits. `LIT-230` cites the account by name, reasons that denser
solutions should mean fewer directions suffice, and measures exactly that at
0.5B, 1.5B and 3B. That is an independent group confirming a *consequence* —
arguably better evidence than a repeat, and **not the evidence the condition
asked for**: different measurement, same family, no prediction of the
threshold. The document now states all of that and stays `Proposed`.

Writing this down is the point. A condition met is a promotion; a condition
approached from an unexpected angle is a judgement call, and the judgement
call is where the bar moves without anyone deciding to move it.

**Two practices came out of readings rather than out of the papers' headlines.**
`SOTA-210` exists because two groups, independently, measured the same
thing the post-training literature does not report — that RLVR raises pass@1
and lowers pass@k, often below the base model. `SOTA-211` exists because
two groups reached one instruction from unrelated arguments: an empirical
variance diagnostic showing the antithetic second evaluation buys nothing when
responses are regenerated, and a derivation showing a leave-one-out baseline
preserves the expected field at half the cost. Neither paper's abstract leads
with the thing that became the practice.

**What this pass did not cover.** The line has at least two more members,
both cited by papers filed here and neither read: **Hoy et al. (2026)** and
**Abdi et al. (2026), *Evolutionary strategies at scale lead to catastrophic
forgetting***. The second is the paper `LIT-230`'s entire RQ2 is a reply
to, and the record currently holds the reply without the claim — which is the
shape `DP-004` warns about, arrived at by following citations forward and
never backward. `LIT-231` also cites **Sun et al. (2026)** for a 10×
space-efficiency result, and `LIT-229` cites **Korotyshova et al. (2025)**
for SFT-then-CMA-ES over SVD bases. Four candidates, named here so the next
pass does not have to rediscover them.

On reading depth: all five notes filed today are `Read` and mean it — full
text including appendices, with two exceptions stated in the notes themselves.
`NOTE-080` takes EGGROLL's Theorem 2 at its stated result and rate
without checking the Edgeworth expansion behind it, and `NOTE-079` takes
`LIT-232`'s resolvent derivation at its stated result without verifying
the conservativity theorem's proof. Both are recorded in the `Limitations`
sections where a reader will meet them.

<a id="20260915191053"></a>

## Following the citations backward, and the boundary that fell out of it

*2026-09-15 19:10:53 · record*

Ten papers now. The four added here were all named in the previous pass's
"what this did not cover" section, which is the first time this record has
closed a gap it had written down rather than rediscovering one — and the
readings changed more than the previous three passes combined.

**The record had filed an answer before the question.** `LIT-230`'s second
research question is, in its entirety, a reply to Abdi et al.: does ES's large
parameter drift cause catastrophic forgetting? The record acquired that reply
two passes ago and acquired the paper it replies to today. `LIT-239`
(ESSA) is the same failure at the other end — the earliest paper in the whole
line, July 2025, filed last, after everything that came after it.

Both have one cause. Every pass so far started from a paper and followed its
citations *forward*, to what cited it or what it responded to among things
already filed. Nothing ever asked **what does this paper cite that we do not
have**, which is a different query with a different answer, and the two gaps
it left were a paper the record was already arguing with and the paper the
line begins at. [DP-004](../design-principles.md#dp-4) is about exactly this and did not prevent it, because
knowing that a query has a complement does not tell you to run the complement.
**The cheap fix, written here so the next pass inherits it: after filing a
paper, list its references that the record lacks.** It takes one grep of the
bibliography.

**The most valuable thing in this pass is a table nobody set out to build.**
Sorting all eight ES-versus-RL comparisons by model size:

- GRPO ahead, 1B and 1.5B — Abdi et al.
- Direct ES "highly ineffective", 0.5B and 1.5B — Hyper-ES
- ES ahead in most cells, 1.5B–8B — Neural Thickets
- ES highest on 4 of 4 tasks, 4B — Hoy et al.
- ES ahead on pass@k, ≤7B — Ba et al.
- ES ahead on pass@k, 7B–32B — Hayes et al.

**Every negative is at or below 1.5B. Every positive is at or above it.** Six
groups, mostly not citing each other and none testing `THEORY-006`, recovered
the threshold that account names. That is a real finding and it arrived as a
*side effect of filing*, not from reading any single paper — which is the
argument for a record like this one existing at all.

It is also the most dangerous kind of finding, and both documents say so: it
is read across papers differing in task, tuning and implementation; it is
post-hoc; and it is exactly what an account's author would want to see.
Nobody has run one protocol on both sides of the line, and until someone does
this is suggestive.

**`THEORY-006` has now come close three times and been promoted none.** A
confirmed prediction (population size falling with scale), a mechanism
(functional sparsity), and now the boundary. The condition asks for the
density measurement repeated by an unconnected group on a different family, or
a mechanism predicting where the transition sits, and none of the three is
that. Holding the line a third time is uncomfortable enough that it is worth
naming the discomfort: **either the account is genuinely unconfirmed, or the
condition is asking for an experiment nobody has reason to run while its
consequences keep turning up on their own.** The document takes the first
reading and flags the second, and deliberately does not decide — a condition
rewritten by whoever wants it met is not a condition, and that principle has
been tested twice in this line now.

**Hoy et al. retired an argument rather than winning it.** Three papers here
had measured ES's parameter drift and drawn three conclusions: it causes
forgetting, it is functionally sparse and harmless, it proves the search finds
nothing. The decomposition — an on-manifold component that changes the loss
and an off-manifold random walk that cannot, scaling as `σ²dT/N` — says all
three are describing the same object. The disagreement was never about the
measurement; it was about what each group happened to have measured alongside
it, and over what horizon.

That is the second time in this line that an apparent contradiction turned out
to be two groups measuring different things. The first was Hyper-ES's lemma
about a *direction* against Ba et al.'s sparse *subspace*. **A record that
holds both sides is what makes these visible; a summary of either one alone
would have read as settled.**

**One filing decision worth recording.** ESSA is ES over a few hundred
SFT-initialized singular values. `SOTA-154` recommends ES over the *full*
parameter space in place of policy-gradient RL. Filing ESSA as support for
that practice would have been easy and wrong, and the note says so explicitly
— same method family, different recommendation. What ESSA does instead is turn
the subspace approach into a line: it and Hyper-ES arrived independently,
eighteen months apart, at *seed a low-dimensional subspace with gradients,
then search it gradient-free*. Two independent arrivals is a better argument
for the approach than either paper's numbers, and it means `SOTA-154`'s
`contested` reading is a live methodological disagreement rather than one
group's objection.

**What this pass did not cover.** The line is now filed to the edges this
record can see, but three things are open and cheap. The bibliography sweep
described above has not been run on any of the ten papers. `ARXIV-2605.30148`
(*Overcoming Forgetting in LLM Fine-Tuning with Evolution Strategies*) turned
up in the search for Abdi et al. and is, by title, the remedy paper for the
problem `SOTA-213` addresses from theory — it was not read, and it is the
obvious next thing. And `LIT-235`'s linear-mode-connectivity result, if it
generalizes, is a claim about post-training reaching one basin regardless of
optimizer, which is worth far more than the use this line makes of it and has
no document of its own.

<a id="20260915192755"></a>

## A practice corrected before it shipped, and a condition finally met

*2026-09-15 19:27:55 · record*

Eleven papers. This one was named in the previous pass's uncovered list and
read for that reason, and it moved two documents that were still sitting
unmerged in the same pull request.

**A practice was wrong and got corrected before anyone could act on it.**
`SOTA-213` was filed an hour earlier as a stopping rule: stop ES
post-training when the target task converges, because drift keeps accumulating
and the gains do not. The reasoning was sound given what the record held.
`LIT-237` ran Countdown to 500 iterations, the task converged near 200,
and *averaged* prior-task accuracy fell across the whole run. Drift is linear
in steps. Therefore stop.

`LIT-238` tracks the prior tasks **individually rather than averaged** and
the picture inverts: HellaSwag drops about 8% over the first 300 iterations and
**returns to its original level by the final iteration**. MMLU-Pro and
ARC-Challenge do the same. ProofWriter runs it upside down, improving and then
settling back. A stopping rule fitted to the average would stop at the bottom
of the dip — the single worst point on the curve.

The lesson is not about evolution strategies. **An average over a set of
measurements can invert the sign of the effect you are inferring from it**, and
a practice derived from one is only as good as the disaggregation nobody ran.
The durable half of the original claim — spend budget on population rather
than steps — survived and is now confirmed directly, which is why this was a
rewrite rather than a retirement.

It was also caught by luck. The paper was in the uncovered list because a
search for something else returned it, and it was read because the previous
pass wrote down what it had not covered. **Writing down the gap is what made
the correction possible**, which is the one process claim these entries can
actually support.

**On correcting in place rather than retiring.** The record's rule is to
retire by changing status and never by deleting, and this practice was
rewritten with its title changed rather than marked `Rejected` with a
successor. The distinction is that it had not landed: it exists only in an
open pull request, and the claim was never one the record made. Filing a
`Rejected` document for a recommendation that was never published would put
something in the attic that nobody ever took out of it. The wrong version is
in this entry and in the changelog instead, which is where a reader looking
for the reasoning will find it.

That reasoning does not extend to anything already on `main`. Once a document
has merged, the rule applies without exception.

**`THEORY-008` is `Active`, and it is the first promotion in this line
that was clean.** Its condition asked for the `σ²dT/N` scaling measured by an
independent group, on a transformer at a different scale, with the
population-size dependence tested directly rather than inferred. That is
Table 1 and Figure 6 of this paper: no shared authors, Qwen2.5-3B rather than
Qwen3-4B, population 30 → 128 halving the update norm — which is what an
inverse dependence of the squared norm on `N` predicts for a 4.3× increase —
and prior-task degradation falling monotonically across three population
sizes.

Worth contrasting with `THEORY-006`, which has now been approached three times
and promoted none. The difference is not that one account is better supported
in some vague sense; it is that **`THEORY-008`'s condition named a
quantity and an operation** — raise `N`, watch drift fall — and `THEORY-006`'s
named a measurement that nobody has reason to repeat. A condition that
specifies an experiment someone would run anyway gets met; one that specifies
an experiment only a partisan would run does not. That is a claim about how to
write `promote_when`, and it is the most transferable thing in this entry.

**One refinement that improves the account it confirms.** Even at population
256 or with an anchor penalty, ES update norms stay an order of magnitude
above GRPO's — while the prior-task KL divergence becomes comparable. So the
harm is not carried by the size of the walk: "it is the randomness of the
drift unconstrained by the target task that leads to prior task forgetting for
ES, rather than the magnitude of updates alone." Three papers in this record
had reached for update norm or update sparsity as the explanatory variable.
None of them was the right one.

**What this pass did not cover.** One new name: **Liang et al. (2026)**, cited
here for low-dimensional curvature of fine-tuning landscapes as the reason
very small populations suffice at billion scale. That is `THEORY-006`'s
subject approached from a third direction and it is not in the record. It is
the only outstanding reference from this paper.

Also still unrun: the bibliography sweep the previous entry prescribed —
after filing a paper, list its references the record lacks. It was prescribed
and then not performed on any of the eleven papers, which is its own small
demonstration that a process note in a journal entry is not a process.

<a id="20260915194321"></a>

## An independence claim that was never checked, and the paper that exposed it

*2026-09-15 19:43:21 · record*

Twelve papers. This one was named in the previous pass's uncovered list, read
for that reason, and the first useful thing it produced was not in its own
abstract — it was in its bibliography.

**The record spent four passes calling a paper independent without opening its
author list.** `SOTA-154` was promoted on `LIT-233`, and the promotion turned
entirely on that paper being an outside check: "an independent group", "a
group with no stake in the result", "nobody here wanted ES to win". The
practice's own condition had excluded "further results from the same group",
so the classification was load-bearing.

**Yulu Gan, `LIT-233`'s first author, is the second author of `LIT-211`.**
It is in `LIT-211`'s author list, in `LIT-233`'s bibliography, and in the
related-work section where that paper cites its own prior work. Nothing was
hidden. Four passes read around it.

The reason is worth naming because it is general. **Independence was inferred
from affiliation and framing** — a different institution, a different senior
author, a paper about something else, the ES comparison arriving as a baseline
rather than as a claim. Every one of those is a proxy, and all of them pointed
the same way, which is exactly when a proxy stops being questioned. The actual
test is one line: *is any author of the new paper an author of the old one?*
It costs a glance at two author lists and it was never run.

**The correction that matters is not to the status.** `SOTA-154` stays
`Active`, because Hoy et al. at 4B with both arms swept and ES highest on all
four tasks is a clean independent positive, and Ba et al., EGGROLL and ESSAM
share no author with `LIT-211` either. The practice would have reached the
same place. **But it would not have got there when it did, on what it did**,
and a record whose promotions rest on misread provenance is failing at the one
thing it exists to do. The consensus note is now tallied by authorship rather
than by institution, and doing that moved four of eight positive results
inside the line they had been counted as independent of.

The corollary, and it belongs beside `DP-005`: **counting is only as good as
the equivalence class you count over.** That principle separates adoption from
evidence; this is the same failure a level down, where several "independent"
results turn out to be one group's line with different mastheads.

**A second thing this paper corrected, in the opposite direction.**
`SOTA-213` has now been rewritten twice in this branch. It began as a
stopping rule, was rewritten when the prior-task dip turned out to recover,
and is rewritten again here — because rise-then-decay means the *target*
reward really does peak and then degrade, so early stopping is right after
all, for a different curve. Prior-task accuracy dips and recovers; target
reward rises and falls. Two curves, two answers, and the first two drafts each
had one of them.

That is three versions of one practice in one afternoon, and it is not a sign
the practice was badly conceived. It is a sign of what filing a line **in
citation order rather than publication order** does: each paper arrived
already answered by one the record had not read yet. Liang et al. is January,
Hoy is April, Schweighofer is May; the record met them backwards.

**On `THEORY-006` and `THEORY-007`, which are not rivals.** They look
like competing explanations of the same phenomenon and they are not, because
`LIT-233` says so itself: the thicket is a broad pretrained basin intersected
with a low-dimensional, degenerate set of task directions, and it cites Liang
for the second half. **The record filed the later paper first and would have
filed them as rivals had the citation not been checked** — the same failure as
the authorship one, caught this time because reading the related-work section
is part of a full reading.

Their one real disagreement is about scale, and it is methodological rather
than substantive: `LIT-233` fixes `σ = 1e-3` at every model size and finds
density rising 0% to 64% across 0.5B–32B; `LIT-236` picks a viable `σ`
per model and finds accessibility flat across 0.5B–7B. A perturbation scale
that suits a 32B model need not suit a 0.5B one, which would produce exactly
this pattern with no disagreement about the geometry. **That also weakens the
scale-boundary table this record built two passes ago**, whose low end may be
a tuning artifact rather than a threshold. The table stays, with the competing
reading beside it.

**What this pass did not cover.** No new names came out of this paper's
references that the record lacks — the first time that has been true in this
line. What remains outstanding is the same two items as last time, both now
overdue: the bibliography sweep prescribed two entries ago and still not run
on any of the twelve papers, and `LIT-235`'s linear-mode-connectivity
result, which if it generalizes is a claim about post-training reaching one
basin regardless of optimizer and still has no document of its own.

And one new one, cheap and specific: **check authorship overlap when filing a
paper into an existing line**, and record the answer rather than the
impression. It would have caught this in the pass that introduced it.

<a id="20260915194938"></a>

## The bibliography sweep, run at last: what twelve papers cite that the record does not hold

*2026-09-15 19:49:38 · record*

Two entries ago this record prescribed a fix for the gap that let it file a
reply before the claim it answers: **after filing a paper, list its references
that the record lacks.** The next entry observed that the prescription had not
been carried out and called that "its own small demonstration that a process
note in a journal entry is not a process." Here it is, run.

## The query, stated so the next person can run it again

For each of the twelve papers in the evolution-strategies line, parse the
bibliography out of the arXiv HTML (`<li id="bib.bibNN">` list items),
extract every arXiv identifier appearing in each entry, and difference the
union against every `arxiv:` field in `record/literature.d/`.

- **532 bibliography entries** across the twelve.
- **144 distinct arXiv identifiers** extracted.
- **227 arXiv identifiers** currently in the record.
- **117 of the 144 are not in the record.**

No script is committed for this. The project removed its helper scripts
deliberately ([#41](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/41)) and `pyproject.toml` says what remains is the frozen
migration; a sweep that runs four times a year does not earn a maintained
artifact. The paragraph above is the artifact.

## What the query cannot see, which is most of it

**Only 45% of the bibliography entries carry an arXiv identifier at all** —
245 of 532 did; the rest are journal and conference references. Everything
classical in this line is therefore invisible to this sweep: Rechenberg (1973),
Schwefel (1977), Hansen and Ostermeier (2001) on CMA-ES, McCloskey and Cohen
(1989) on catastrophic forgetting, Kirkpatrick et al. (2017) on elastic weight
consolidation. Several are cited by four or more of the twelve.

This is [DP-004](../design-principles.md#dp-4) operating on the pass that was written to fix an instance of
[DP-004](../design-principles.md#dp-4). The complement of "references carrying an arXiv id" is not empty,
and running the filter harder does not sample it. **The honest statement is
that this sweep found what an arXiv-shaped query can find**, and a second pass
keyed to author-year strings would return a different and older set.

## The headline, and it is worse than the gap that prompted the sweep

**`ARXIV-1703.03864` — Salimans, Ho, Chen, Sidor and Sutskever, *Evolution
Strategies as a Scalable Alternative to Reinforcement Learning* — is cited by
ten of the twelve papers and is not in this record.**

The record holds nine papers descending from it, a practice recommending the
technique it introduced ([SOTA-154](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-154.md)), two theory documents explaining why
that technique works, and not the paper. This is exactly [DP-007](../design-principles.md#dp-7)'s "trunk with
no document": every fork in the line has an entry because every fork was
somebody's contribution, and the thing all ten take for granted has none.

**`ARXIV-1707.06347` — PPO — is cited by six of the twelve and is also
absent.** That gap was noticed by hand two passes ago and written into a
curation entry as a suspected instance. The sweep confirms it and puts a
number on it.

## The shortlist

Ranked within groups by how many of the twelve cite each. Everything here is
missing from the record.

**The trunk of the method.** Filing these is what [DP-007](../design-principles.md#dp-7) asks for.

**The low-dimensional-structure line, which [THEORY-007](../../record/theory.d/THEORY-007.md) rests on and does not
cite.** `ARXIV-1812.04754` (Gur-Ari et al., *Gradient descent happens in a
tiny subspace*, 2018) states something close to that account's central claim
eight years earlier. With it: `ARXIV-2012.13255` (Aghajanyan et al., intrinsic
dimensionality), `ARXIV-1804.08838` (Li et al., intrinsic dimension of
objective landscapes), `ARXIV-1706.04454` (Sagun et al., Hessian of
over-parametrized networks — the "bulk plus outliers" source), and
`ARXIV-2602.04118` (Morris et al., *Learning to reason in 13 parameters*).

**Method ingredients the record uses without holding.**
`ARXIV-2010.01412` (Foret et al., SAM — what [LIT-240](../../record/literature.d/LIT-240.md) transposes into zeroth
order) and `ARXIV-2203.11171` (Wang et al., self-consistency — the
majority-vote step inside [SOTA-212](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-212.md) and the baseline in [SOTA-210](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-210.md)).

**Benchmarks, model reports and infrastructure**, which this record has never
systematically filed and which the sweep surfaces in volume: GSM8K
(`ARXIV-2110.14168`, 9 of 12), MBPP, the Qwen2.5 technical report,
HellaSwag, ARC, GPQA, MATH, HumanEval, ROCStories, and verl
(`ARXIV-2409.19256`). **Whether these belong here is a scope question the
record has never answered in writing**, and the sweep is the first time the
cost of not answering it has been visible: they are 9 of the 27 most-cited
missing references, and every pass has silently declined them.

## What this changes about how passes should run

The sweep took minutes and the gap it found is the largest single omission in
this line. Two things follow.

**Run it at filing time, not as a separate pass.** The reason it kept not
happening is that it was written down as a future task rather than as part of
what filing a paper means. A note in a journal entry is a reminder; a step in
the filing procedure is a process. This entry is still only the former.

**Count the citations rather than reading them.** The useful output was not
the 117-item list, which nobody will act on, but the ranking. *Cited by ten of
twelve and absent* is a finding; *cited once and absent* is a reading list.
The ranking is what turned a dump into the Salimans result.

## What this pass did not do

It filed nothing. Every entry above is a candidate, and the top two —
Salimans et al. and PPO — are the ones the record should not go another pass
without, on [DP-007](../design-principles.md#dp-7)'s argument rather than on any judgement about their
quality.

## Filing the trunk, and what it turned out to have already said

*2026-09-15 20:03:25 · record*

The sweep prescribed two papers and the record filed them. Both readings
found something the record did not know, and in both cases what they found was
that a document already here was newer than its idea.

**Salimans et al. §3.2 is `THEORY-007`.** That account — filed two hours ago
from a 2026 paper — holds that ES scales because what matters is not the
ambient parameter count but a low-dimensional effective structure. The 2017
paper:

> However, it is important to note that this does not mean that larger neural
> networks will perform worse than smaller networks when optimized using ES:
> what matters is the difficulty, or intrinsic dimension, of the optimization
> problem.

It gives the argument (concatenate a regression's features with themselves:
parameters double, difficulty does not, ES behaves identically given `σ` and
the learning rate halved) and the observation (larger Atari networks did
slightly better). `LIT-236` adds a mechanism, a measurement across scales, and
the connection to rise-then-decay, all of which are real contributions. **But
the record filed that account without knowing its central claim was nine years
old**, and would have gone on presenting it as new.

The same shape for PPO. Three practices here modify it — `SOTA-145` removes
its critic, `SOTA-146` corrects an objective descended from its clipped ratio,
`SOTA-129` makes the family a recipe stage — and none could cite it. Reading
it turns up a detail no descendant mentions: the ES line grid-searches PPO's
KL coefficient `β`, and PPO's own §4 reports the KL-penalized variant as the
**worse** of the two its authors tested.

**The general form, and it is what `DP-007` is about from a new angle.** That
principle says the agreed trunk goes unfiled because agreement has no arrival.
The corollary this pass adds: **while the trunk is missing, its claims get
re-filed as though they were new by whoever restates them.** A record that
holds only the branches cannot tell a contribution from a restatement, and the
error runs in the flattering direction — every paper looks more original than
it is, because the thing it is building on is not here to compare against.

That is a sharper reason to file trunks than pedagogy. It is not that a reader
wants the foundational paper; it is that **without it the record cannot
grade the ones it has.**

## On what counts as evidence for a practice, revisited

Filing Salimans also settles something the record had been asserting on
[LIT-211](../../record/literature.d/LIT-211.md)'s authority. That ES "tolerates long-horizon and delayed rewards"
has been in this record since `SOTA-154` was filed, as a claim about a claim.
The argument is in §3.1 here: the policy-gradient score term is a sum of `T`
uncorrelated pieces so its variance grows nearly linearly with episode length,
while the ES term is independent of `T`. Four of the five arguments `SOTA-154`
makes for itself originate in this paper, and the practice has been making
them second-hand.

`introduced_by:` stays on [LIT-211](../../record/literature.d/LIT-211.md) and the reasoning is worth keeping: this
paper recommends ES over policy gradients for **control tasks trained from
scratch**, and the practice recommends it for **LLM fine-tuning**, which this
paper does not attempt and whose feasibility the field doubted for eight
years. The doubt is the evidence that they are different claims. Filing the
ancestor makes that distinction visible rather than dissolving it.

## The scope question, answered

`ADR-032` records what the sweep forced: benchmarks, model reports and
infrastructure are admissible `LIT` documents. Three things about how that
decision was reached are worth keeping.

**The record was already half-doing it.** [LIT-119](../../record/literature.d/LIT-119.md), [LIT-130](../../record/literature.d/LIT-130.md) and [LIT-222](../../record/literature.d/LIT-222.md) are
model reports and a whitepaper, already `Active`. The practice registry counts
model reports as adoption evidence in `consensus:`. So the boundary would have
had to be drawn between things the record already treats identically — which
is [DP-008](../../docs/design-principles.md#dp-8)'s warning realized: the scope existed in what the corpus happened
to contain, not in anything anyone decided.

**Nothing in the vocabulary changes**, and that is the test. A benchmark paper
is `analysis-and-evaluation` by that topic's own blurb; a model report takes
the topic of what it reports on; infrastructure is `systems-optimization`.
[DP-008](../../docs/design-principles.md#dp-8) says a category added to admit a single document is how a scope
stops being one — the converse also holds, and a scope change needing no new
category is one the vocabulary was already sized for.

**The trigger stays narrow.** Something in the record has to cite it. A
benchmark nothing here is argued on has no standing to record, and the ADR
says so, because the failure mode of this decision is a reading list that is
mostly instruments.

## What this pass did not do

The backlog the ADR creates is named and unfiled: GSM8K (cited by 9 of 12),
the Qwen2.5 technical report (4), MBPP (3), verl (3). The sweep's ranking is
the queue.

And the sweep itself still has the hole its own entry described: **only 45% of
bibliography entries carry an arXiv identifier**, so the classical ES
literature — Rechenberg 1973, Schwefel 1977, Hansen and Ostermeier 2001 — is
invisible to it. Salimans et al. cites all three in its first paragraph on ES.
Filing the trunk has not reached the roots, and the query that would is a
different one.

<a id="20260915214538"></a>

## The schema was the tell, and I read it as evidence of a stranger

*2026-09-15 21:45:38 · record · migration*

Seventy-four paper notes arrived from another project. I checked every
identifier against arXiv and CrossRef before filing anything, found three
notes bound to the wrong paper and one citation invented outright, and
concluded that the batch was a secondary source whose claims could not be
trusted. So I filed all sixty-eight papers at `Deferred`, filed no readings,
and sent all 187 recommendations to an issue on the grounds that a practice
may not be sourced to a paper nobody here has read.

The rule is right. The premise was wrong: **they were my own readings, made in
a different session under a different agenda.** Nobody had to tell me the
rule; I had to be told the readings were mine.

## What I had in front of me

The incoming schema, from the batch's own `SCHEMA.md`:

    contribution, key_insight, assumptions, key_results, claims, method,
    concepts, connections, recommendations, research_implications,
    limitations, open_questions

The section headings of every NOTE document in this record:

    Contribution, Key insight, Assumptions, Key results, Claims, Method,
    Concepts, Connections, Recommendations, Bearing on the record,
    Limitations, Open questions

Twelve fields, twelve sections, same order, eleven of them the same name. I
read that table, wrote it into a comparison, and did not draw the conclusion.
The thing I did instead was notice that the batch's schema described
`recommendations` as "project-agnostic" and treat that as a *claim by a
stranger to be checked* rather than as a note I had left myself.

## The reasoning error, stated plainly

I had four pieces of evidence and they pointed two ways.

Pointing at "stranger": a different project, a different agenda, an
identifier bound to the wrong paper three times, and a citation that resolves
to nothing.

Pointing at "mine": a schema that is this record's schema, down to field
order.

I weighted the first four and never priced the fifth, because I had a query
shaped like *how much can I trust this?* and a query finds only defects it is
shaped like ([DP-004](../design-principles.md#dp-4)). "Whose work is this?" was never asked, so the
one piece of evidence that answered it went past as an interesting
coincidence.

The nearest precedent in this record is a week old and is the inverse.
Filing `LIT-233` I inferred a paper's *independence* from affiliation, senior
authorship and framing, three proxies agreeing, and never ran the author-list
check that would have contradicted them. Here I inferred a batch's
*foreignness* from provenance, agenda and error rate, three proxies agreeing,
and never asked who wrote the schema. Same failure, opposite sign: proxies
that agree with each other feel like corroboration and are one observation.

## What the findings turned out to mean

The identifier errors are real and none of them survived as a reason to
withhold a reading.

- **`1805.01361`** is not a bad note about a stranger's paper. It is a second
  reading of `1804.06561`, filed against a stranger's identifier. Both
  readings are genuine and they differ — one is precise about the theorem
  statements, the other reaches for the McKean-Vlasov framing. They are merged
  into one note.
- **`1906.08632`**'s reading is of the paper its identifier names. Only the
  title field was taken from a different Goldt paper.
- **`2102.11742`** is the one that does not rebind: the reading names no paper
  its content matches, and its own first paragraph says so. Filed `Deferred`,
  no note. This is the single case where the first decision was right, and it
  is right for one paper rather than sixty-eight.
- **Wolfowitz (1963)** was given a journal, a volume, a page range and a DOI
  that returns 404. That one is not a labelling slip, and it is why metadata
  in the port comes from resolvers in every case and from the reading in none.

## What actually did not port, and why

Not trust — **scope**.

The field that does not survive is `research_implications`, which answers five
questions from that project's `synthesis/research_agenda.md`. Seventy of those
were replaced by a `## Bearing on the record` section written fresh, answering
this record's question instead: what could a practice here rest on, and is
there one.

Twenty-three of the 187 recommendations are marked in place as not filed.
Seventeen name that project's own system and experiments despite the schema
calling the field project-agnostic — which is worth noticing, because it means
a field I labelled "preserved for reuse beyond this project" was not, and the
label did not stop me writing project-specific advice into it. Six are advice
to a theorist about proof technique. They are struck, not deleted.

## What this pass still has not covered

**The readings themselves were not re-verified against the papers.** The
identifier check was on titles and authors. Nothing compared a single entry
under `key_results` or `claims` against the paper it is about. That was the
honest limit of the first pass and it is unchanged by learning whose work it
is — being my own reading makes it portable, not correct.

**Two papers now have two readings and only one is filed.** `LIT-017`
(McCandlish) and `LIT-028` (Kaplan) already had notes. The incoming readings
of both are mostly about curve-fitting for another project's experiments, so
little was lost, but nothing compared them.

**Four of the seventy-four files arrived truncated mid-scalar**, at the end of
`limitations` or `research_implications`. Two lost a partial limitation; two
lost only dropped material. Recovered by discarding the incomplete line.

**The practices filed are seven of a hundred and sixty-four candidates.** They
are the ones where the claim is crisp, the paper is the right place to source
it, and nothing here already says it. The rest is still a backlog, and it is
now a backlog of *reading already done* rather than of reading still owed —
which is a much cheaper thing to owe.
